record.name: Grid interconnection and deliverable electrical capacity
record.shortName: Grid interconnection and deliverable electrical capacity
record.role: Connects facility demand to location-specific network, equipment and operating readiness.
record.description: A site’s proposed demand must fit a real electricity network at a real location. Interconnection planning examines service arrangements and required infrastructure rather than treating a national generation total as locally available power. Substations, transformers, transmission and distribution work have their own schedules, while load forecasts assess how much proposed demand is likely to materialize. PJM’s 2026 methodology discusses screening large-load requests and adjusting forecasts. A signed capacity agreement, completed electrical equipment and permission to operate are different states. Backup energy and demand response can support operation but do not automatically replace a continuous grid connection.

record.tradeoff: A site with favorable land or fiber may need longer electrical upgrades; on-site support equipment adds cost and operational dependencies.

record.scale: Manufacturing supply to commissioned hall; time-dependent model
mechanism: Define the facility load boundary and the expected time-dependent demand.
Identify the required grid connection and screen the project against duplicate or speculative requests.
Track studies, service commitments and required network or substation work separately.
Verify equipment installation and operational acceptance before assigning deliverable capacity.
Model backup duration and demand-response constraints without treating them as unlimited continuous supply.
record.misconception: An announced megawatt connection or generation project is not proof that a specific hall can draw that power today.

check.question: A battery can deliver 20 MWh of usable energy at the load-side boundary while supplying a constant 10 MW. What is its ideal duration?
check.explanation: 20 MWh divided by 10 MW gives two hours. Conversion losses and reserved energy have already been accounted for in the stated load-side usable energy.

science.title: Backup duration
science.explanation: Eusable is energy deliverable at the load-side boundary in MWh, Pload is constant output power in MW, and t is hours.
science.assumptions: Positive constant load; usable energy already accounts for conversion losses, reserves and the stated battery condition. Changing load, temperature or degradation requires a revised usable-energy estimate.

record.learningObjective: Separate proposed demand, local electrical service and backup duration.
record.engineeringExample: Synthetic commissioning plan has racks arriving in March and a required transformer accepted in June. The electrical readiness gate can delay operation despite the earlier hardware delivery.
record.evidenceNotes: PJM is one regional example, not global interconnection law. The source’s inconsistent winter headline is excluded; no unverified local queue position is claimed.
record.scope: Propagate a stated facility power budget, PUE, readiness and utilization to illustrative work; detailed conversion, battery, cooling and grid models are not included.

variables.meaning: Energy usable at the declared load-side boundary

formalEquations.text: Backup duration is already-usable energy divided by constant load power.
formalEquations.note: This load-side energy convention differs from a stored-energy input that still needs conversion efficiency.
